newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FORECAST - Aussie bonds have hard act to follow.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FORECAST - Aussie bonds have hard act to follow.

text.p: The 1/4 point spike in long-dated Australian government bond yields in the first few trading days of the year could be a sign of things to come over 1997.

Even if this sell-off proves to be a temporary phenomenon, analysts believe that the market will find 1996 a hard act to follow, a year which saw yields drop to their lowest level since early 1994 and the yield spread to the U.S. slashed.
Although the inflation outlook for Australia remains positive, concerns over growth both domestically and in the United States could put the market under some pressure.
"There's no doubt that inflation will stay low for a while," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at Macquarie Bank.

"But by the end of this year I would imagine that a lot of the good news on inflation will be behind us and we may start to see a little bit of concern about the current account deficit as growth recovers," he added.

A Reuters poll of 22 economists taken on Friday showed the median forecast for the 10-year bond yield at the end of this year at 8.0 percent compared with the current level of just over 7.5 percent. However, expectations were fairly wide, ranging from 6.75 to 8.60 percent.
The 10-year bond yield flirted with 7.0 percent for the first time in nearly three years in December, some 120 basis points below where its started 1996.
Last year was also significant in a wider sense, with Australia shedding its label as a high inflation economy, along with a host of other positive fundamentals.
Some economists believe that the benign inflation outlook will keep yields low, and may even push them through the elusive 7.0 percent barrier at some stage during the year.

But this is likely to hinge on the Reserve Bank cutting official interest rates again -- an action that the central bank undertook three times in the second half of 1996 to reduce rates to 6.0 percent.
At the time of the last rate cut on December 11, the Reserve Bank said it expected underlying inflation to remain under 2.5 percent, and within its target, for the rest of fiscal year 1996/97.
It also expected a good inflation performance for 1997/98.

"We're still factoring in another rate cut....We really think that low inflation and moderate wage growth will continue and growth won't really pickup until late in the year," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Group.
Westpac sees the 10-year bond yield at 6.75 percent at year-end, possibly at 6.50 percent midway through the year.
Improved inflation has seen a dramatic tightening in the 10-year yield spread to the U.S., falling at one stage to around 80 basis points (b.p.) from 250 b.p at the start of 1996.
But the Reuters poll showed that this narrowing trend could be at an end -- with the median forecast centring on 140 b.p. from a current level of just over 110 b.p.
Again, estimates were wide ranging, from just 40 b.p. to 225 b.p.

"What we see are domestic cyclical forces picking up here along with a pickup in the current account deficit, and concerns about inflation, even though inflation is going to remain low," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura.

Nomura, which puts the spread at 225 b.p. at year-end, see this sharp deterioration also reflecting its belief that current concerns over the U.S. economy overheating are exaggerated, and that it will slow of its own accord, which could even see the next move by the Federal Reserve being an easing in policy.
Westpac, meanwhile, believes there is still room for a further spread narrowing, although the main bulk of the tightening has been done.
"We think it could get down to 75/80 (b.p.), but certainly the big moves are behind us and most of the juice has been squeezed from the lemon," Westpac's Peters added.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
